paragraphs.ncert_ref: Section 8.2, Cell Theory. Page and line: not verified.
paragraphs.meaning: Every living thing is built from cells, and the cell is the basic unit of life. Schleiden and Schwann gave this idea. Virchow added the second half: new cells do not appear from nothing, they come from cells that already exist.

words.meaning: Every cell comes from an existing cell.
words.breakdown: omnis = every, cellula = small cell, e = from
words.trap: Students credit this line to Schleiden and Schwann. It is Virchow's addition.

words.meaning: The smallest unit that carries out the activities of life.
words.breakdown: Latin cella = small room. Robert Hooke used the word in 1665 after seeing boxlike compartments in cork.
words.trap: Hooke saw only the walls of dead cork cells, never the living contents.

paragraphs.visual_alt: Top: six squares forming a block, labelled as the Schleiden and Schwann idea that bodies are made of cells. Bottom: one square with an arrow to two squares, labelled as Virchow's idea that cells come from cells.
paragraphs.hook: Schleiden and Schwann counted the bricks. Virchow noticed every new brick is baked from an old one.
paragraphs.exam_note: NEET asks who said what: who proposed the cell theory and who added the new-cells rule. It also appears as an exceptions question about viruses.
paragraphs.trap: Schleiden and Schwann proposed the cell theory. Virchow modified it. Options often swap the names.

recall.q: Who explained that new cells form from pre-existing cells?
recall.why: Virchow added that cells divide and new cells come from existing ones, which gave the cell theory its final shape. Schleiden and Schwann gave the first part, that bodies are made of cells.

recall.q: What did Robert Hooke see in a thin slice of cork in 1665?
recall.why: He saw many small boxlike compartments, the walls of dead cork cells, and called them cells. He did not see living contents or nuclei.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Section 8.4, Prokaryotic Cells. Page and line: not verified.
paragraphs.meaning: A prokaryotic cell has no nucleus wrapped in a membrane. Its DNA lies in an open region of the cytoplasm called the nucleoid, and it has no membrane-bound organelles. It still has ribosomes, and many bacteria also carry small extra rings of DNA called plasmids.

words.meaning: Describes a cell without a membrane-bound nucleus.
words.breakdown: pro = before, karyon = kernel or nucleus (Greek)
words.trap: Students think prokaryotes have no DNA. They have DNA, just not inside a nuclear membrane.

words.meaning: The region where the DNA of a prokaryote sits.
words.trap: Nucleoid looks like a nucleus but has no membrane around it.

words.meaning: A small circular piece of DNA outside the main DNA.
words.trap: Plasmids are extra DNA. Cells can live without them, but they often carry traits like antibiotic resistance.

paragraphs.visual_alt: A rounded bacterial cell with an outer wall and an inner dashed membrane. Inside are a tangled nucleoid, a small plasmid ring and scattered ribosome dots, each labelled.
paragraphs.hook: A prokaryote is a studio flat: one open room, DNA lying on the floor. A eukaryote has a locked bedroom for the DNA, the nucleus.
paragraphs.exam_note: NEET likes prokaryote versus eukaryote comparisons: ribosome type, nuclear membrane, plasmids and organelles.
paragraphs.trap: No membrane-bound organelles does not mean no ribosomes. Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes, which have no membrane.

recall.q: Which of these is present in a prokaryotic cell?
recall.why: Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes in the cytoplasm. Nucleolus, mitochondria and Golgi apparatus belong to eukaryotic cells.

recall.q: Where is the DNA of a bacterial cell found?
options: In the nucleoid, with no membrane around it
recall.why: Bacterial DNA lies in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm. No membrane separates it from the rest of the cell.
